doc.title: David Weiss interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, May 3, 2022

title: Race and the Cookers' life stories: Billy Harper, Cecil McBee
summary: Asked about race, Weiss recounts Billy Harper's treatment at North Texas State and Cecil McBee's childhood story, and says he is treated well and gets lessons from Billy Hart and George Cables.

story.theme_name: Race and segregation in the jazz life
story.community_name: Segregation on the road and the bandstand

blocks.x: I see. Have they ever talked about back in the earlier parts of their career I think critics and authors sometimes like to make an issue of race in jazz. And I’m wondering if you hear that from these musicians?

I hear stuff about how they’re treated. You know I don’t think it’s in jazz, I think it’s in the world they live in. Like Billy Harper went to North Texas State and so did I. So one of our first conversations was like wow, North Texas State, it was a little different for a little Jewish boy from Queens. And then he told me his story and I’m like [holds up hands]. You know? “I couldn’t live on campus. I had to live in a little shack on the other side of the tracks and I had to walk two miles to school and finally by the third year they let me live on campus but it was like a janitor’s closet. You know they found a place for me because I had made the —” you know, like oh, whoa, okay. I get it. Somebody going like, “You’re Jewish” wasn’t exactly comparable. So I mean — the life, you know so the life, the life, I mean we’re talking about our lives and stuff like that. Cecil McBee told me once when he was a little kid he just tried to make a couple of pennies shining shoes and a couple of cowboys came and picked him up and threw him in a trash can. You know? I mean there is so much stuff that informs who they are. It’s not a barrage of that but when we’re on a long train ride and people are talking about their lives, that’s part of their life. I have nothing comparable you know. But I seem to be able to relate to their world philosophy in a lot of ways. I mean it’s kind of like this knowing, seen it all, you know,

but have found a way to (a) sort of find the beauty in it, (b) you know, be very practical about things. I’ll tend to get more caught up in little things because well I’ll say I’m privileged maybe. I don’t know. But it’s never a thing, you know, they’re very nice to me. You know I think you know in the end people are people. There are differences but I mean I think at this point I don’t have to prove it to them but I think they know my heart’s in the right place. You know? I put — and more importantly it’s a musical thing. If it wasn’t a good musical experience they wouldn’t do it. You know? Or they would let me know. You know? They’re not always on me but sometimes after a gig I can be walking off the stage after the last tune and Billy Hart can say like, “You took one chorus too many on that one, didn’t you?” And I’m like, “Yeah, yeah I did.” You know? The lessons are always there. Or the opposite you know. George Cables after a gig once I remember, “Man, you showed me something on that last —” so you know. So it’s not a constant thing but it’s you know I’m told.
